claims.text: The target materials are near-equiatomic, single-phase high-entropy alloys with random solid-solution microstructures.

A model incorporating atomistic descriptors of configurational disorder and local lattice distortion will identify low-phonon-thermal-conductivity high-entropy alloys more accurately than models based only on averaged elemental properties.
Atomic-scale randomness, bond-length distributions, and local lattice distortions can be represented as descriptors in a machine-learning model.
Atomic disorder and local lattice distortions intensify phonon scattering.
Intensified phonon scattering reduces phonon thermal conductivity.
Local lattice distortion and variations in bonding and atomic-mass distributions contribute to phonon damping.
Explicitly representing atomistic phonon-scattering features will make predicted low thermal conductivities more faithful to measured values.
The proposed model will reduce phonon-thermal-conductivity prediction RMSE by more than 20% relative to models based on averaged elemental properties.
The approach is applicable when the alloys retain uniform solid-solution structures with minimal phase segregation or ordering.
The approach is applicable when atomic-disorder-driven phonon scattering is the dominant thermal-insulation mechanism.
The approach may not improve predictions for alloys whose thermal conduction is dominated by electrons.
Severe phase segregation may invalidate the atomistic disorder descriptors and eliminate the model's predictive advantage.
Time-domain thermoreflectance can be used to obtain an independent experimental benchmark for phonon thermal conductivity in the alloy series.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant RMSE reduction exceeding 20% across the tested alloy range would falsify the hypothesis.
Systematic prediction failure for alloys with high atomic disorder would falsify the hypothesis.
